facts.claim: "Something Better" by The Broken View is a 5:15 track released September 6, 2019. It appears on the band's EP of the same name.
The song is credited as written by Austin Kranick and Tyler Shoemaker.
It is track 3 of the 5-track Something Better EP. Deezer credits Kranick and Shoemaker as writers and composers of the EP's tracks.
Frontman Austin Kranick said he wrote the lyrics about moving on from a toxic relationship. He described the anger of being shut out of someone's life until it becomes an obsession.
Kranick said he hopes listeners in the same situation will find their own 'something' that leads them to a better state of mind.

A Soundscape Notes interview describes the song as having no clear chorus and building through a series of different verses. It calls it the most metal-sounding of the EP's five songs. It also says the song starts to turn toward moving on after the grief and anger of a relationship ending.
Drummer Tyler Shoemaker started the band in 2018. After recording solo work for Austin at Shoemaker's studio, Greyscale Recordings in Malta, NY, he asked Kranick to join.
The band writes and records its own material and has filmed and produced its own music videos. An official music video for "Something Better" was uploaded to YouTube in December 2019.
The band name comes from 'break views' in graphic design, which show how an object works from the inside. A mock-up logo Tyler sent Austin was used for the Something Better EP.
The Broken View is an alternative hard rock band from Saratoga Springs, NY. Their first full album, On the Mend, came out in 2021 after the 2019 Something Better EP. Ordinary Love followed in 2024.

research.lineage: The song sits in the independent alternative hard rock / alternative metal scene of upstate New York, where the band records its own material.

draft:
The most telling line in **Something Better** is a correction: "I'm not insane, I'm only a fool for you." The narrator defends himself before anyone has made the charge, and that tells you how far this has gone. Austin Kranick, The Broken View's frontman, has said he wrote the lyrics about moving on from a toxic relationship. He described the anger of being shut out of someone's life until it turns into an obsession. The song lives inside that obsession, and it doesn't pretend to have gotten out.

Listen to how the refrain is built. A run of lines lets the other person off the hook: you don't have to lose, don't have to lie, don't have to choose, don't have to say goodbye. It sounds generous. Then it flips. The narrator doesn't have to absorb all the time wasted on dishonesty, and then comes the stubborn heart of it: "I will not be the one who never got the chance to change your mind." He's leaving, and he's still arguing his case on the way out. Wounded pride and real longing sit in the same sentence, and neither one gives ground. The bridge lets the bitterness show plainly, "it's all gone sideways," and both of them end up scared and wrecked, but blame never fully lands on one side.

The sound carries that pressure. A distorted guitar holds thick, sustained chords over a bass that keeps the low end planted. The drums push a driving rock groove at a moderate tempo with a hard kick and snare. The vocal is doubled and held long on the notes, clean in tone but with some grit at the edges, as if he's working to keep it together. It's dense and polished, the heaviest of the five songs on the *Something Better* EP. That fits a band from Saratoga Springs, New York, working in the independent alt-hard-rock and alt-metal scene upstate. Drummer Tyler Shoemaker started the band in 2018 after recording Kranick's solo work at his own studio, Greyscale Recordings in Malta, NY. The two wrote the song together, and the band records its own material.

The band name comes from the "break views" of graphic design, drawings that show how an object works from the inside. That's a fair description of what this song does to a breakup. The ending goes long, the title phrase repeated again and again, and at 5:15 some listeners will feel the stretch. But the repetition reads as a mantra more than filler. Kranick has said he hopes people in the same spot find their own "something" that gets them to a better state of mind. The last lines sound like someone still trying to believe it, "before I believe in something better than you," saying it until it might be true.

You keep coming back because the song catches the exact moment when walking away and begging to stay are the same sentence.
